The hybrid-plant-level studies also highlighted how inverter- level GFM behavior is influenced by supervisory plant controls, emphasizing the importance of coordinated tuning. Task 1 also included an engineering evaluation of battery sizing and operational characteristics for GFM functionality. Studies of fast active-power injection, droop response, and current-limiting constraints established that the BESS platform was capable of supporting GFM modes under the targeted disturbance scenarios. This analysis ensured that the chosen GFM implementation was technically feasible and aligned with real-world inverter. Finally, the project completed a detailed reliability and risk analysis through a Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA). Thirty potential failure modes were identified across inverter controls, plant-level coordination, communication dependencies, and weak-grid operational scenarios. The FMEA provided systematic visibility into potential system risks during commissioning and field demonstration, and informed mitigation strategies required before enabling GFM operation at full scale. Taken together, the Task-1 activities delivered a validated technical baseline for GFM deployment at Wheatridge. The metric framework, EMT validation results, BESS sizing assessment, and risk analysis form an integrated understanding of expected GFM performance and establish the engineering foundation necessary for subsequent tuning, commissioning, and system-level evaluation. 7.2 Task 2 - Demonstration Preparatory Work Task 2 focused on preparing the technical and engineering framework to enable safe GFM operation in the hybrid Wheatridge facility. Whereas Task 1 established the analytical foundation for GFM behavior, Task 2 translated those insights into the procedural, tuning, and design elements needed for an eventual field demonstration. A key aspect of this task was developing a structured tuning methodology for GFM controls. The project defined preliminary parameter ranges for voltage-forming loops, angle-control behavior, droop characteristics, and current-limiting functions, ensuring that inverter-level settings would be compatible with both EMT findings and expected coordination with plant-level supervisory control. The tuning work recognized that GFM and GFL units respond differently to grid disturbances; therefore, the tuning needed to emphasize stable multi-resource coordination rather than the optimization of any single inverter. In parallel, the project team conducted a series of engineering design reviews to evaluate hybrid-plant interactions, inverter-level control assumptions, protection coordination, and supervisory-control integration. These reviews were essential for aligning assumptions across OEMs, utility engineers, national-laboratory partners, and plant-operator teams. The reviews also ensured consistency between modeling Page 12 of 36 Award Number: DE-EE0010651 Recipient Name: Portland General Electric assumptions and real-world equipment capabilities, helping prevent discrepancies between simulation-based expectations and field behavior. Task 2 also produced a comprehensive test plan for the future demonstration phase. The plan outlines the types of disturbances, operating conditions, and measurement requirements necessary to evaluate GFM performance across voltage, frequency, and angle-support domains. The plan defines how data will be collected, which events will be analyzed, and what performance indicators will be used to compare GFM behavior against GFL baselines.
